<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:compression}
For every integer $h\ge2$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:exactnu}
 \nu(h,4)=
 \begin{cases}
 \displaystyle\binom{h+2}{2}+(h\bmod2),&2\le h\le10,\\[3pt]
 (h-3)(h-1),&h\ge11.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
The proof for $h\ge17$ is independent of finite enumeration.
The cases $2\le h\le16$ use the complete finite calculation
in Section~\ref{sec:computation}.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:rigidity}
Let $h\ge9$ and put $d_h=(h-3)(h-1)$.
Every integer four-set $A$ with $|hA|=M_h-17$ satisfies
\[
 \operatorname{ndiam}(A)\in\{d_h,d_h+1,d_h+2\}.
\]
Moreover, $\eta_{17}(h)=d_h$. The minimum is attained by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:uniform}
 A_h=
 \begin{cases}
 \{0,h-4,2h-5,d_h\},&h\not\equiv1\pmod3,\\
 \{0,h-3,2h-3,d_h\},&h\equiv1\pmod3.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:asymptotic}
We have $\displaystyle\lim_{h\to\infty}\nu(h,4)/h^2=1$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Divide the second branch of \eqref{eq:exactnu} by $h^2$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:diameter}
If $u,v\in L_A$ are linearly independent, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:product_index}
 [L_A:\mathbb Z u+\mathbb Z v]\,D\le \rho(u)\rho(v).
\end{equation}
Consequently active rank two implies $D\le h^2$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Delete coordinate zero and denote the projected vectors by $u',v'$.
Their cross product is an integer multiple of $(a,b,D)$.
The absolute multiplier is $[L_A:\mathbb Z u+\mathbb Z v]$.
Indeed, a basis of the kernel of the primitive linear form
$(a,b,D)$, together with an integer vector on which the form
is one, is a basis of $\mathbb Z^3$. Its determinant is one up to
sign. Changing the kernel basis to $u',v'$ multiplies the
cross product by the determinant of that change, namely
the lattice index.

For any two coordinates $(x,y)$ of a zero-sum relation of degree $r$,
\[
 |x|\le r,\qquad |y|\le r,\qquad |x+y|\le r.
\]
Indeed the absolute sum over any subset of coordinates is at most
the total positive mass. The unit hexagon described by these three
inequalities has vertices
\[
 (1,0),(1,-1),(0,-1),(-1,0),(-1,1),(0,1).
\]
The absolute determinant of any two vertices is at most one.
By convexity in each argument, this remains true for any two points
of the hexagon. Hence every two-coordinate minor of $u',v'$ has
absolute value at most $\rho(u)\rho(v)$.
The last component of their cross product has absolute value
$[L_A:\mathbb Z u+\mathbb Z v]D$, proving the bound.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:replacement}
Fix $h\ge2$ and $D_0\ge0$. Suppose that every integer four-set
$A$ with $\operatorname{ndiam}(A)>D_0$ has an integer four-set
$B$ satisfying
\[
 |hB|=|hA|,\qquad \operatorname{ndiam}(B)\le D_0.
\]
Then $\nu(h,4)\le D_0$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Take any attainable cardinality and a normalized realization.
If its diameter is at most $D_0$, it already lies in the
required interval. Otherwise, use the stipulated set $B$ and
normalize it. This realizes the same cardinality in
$[0,D_0]\cap\mathbb Z$. Since the cardinality was arbitrary, every
element of $\mathcal R(h,4)$ occurs there.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:fiber_tools}
Let $r$ be the least nonzero relation degree. Suppose $2r>h$
and there are at most four unsigned active directions.
Every representation fiber then has at most three points.
If $E$ is the number of unordered collision edges and $T$
the number of triple fibers, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:edge_count}
 \Delta_h(A)=E-T,\qquad
 E=\sum_{\text{unsigned active }z}M_{h-\rho(z)}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Every active vector is primitive, since a proper divisor would
have degree at most $h/2<r$. Four points in a fiber have six
pair differences, so two agree up to sign.
If their edges share a vertex, an active multiple $2u$ results,
contrary to $2\rho(u)>h$.
If the edges are disjoint, the points form a parallelogram
of shape $\{0,u,v,u+v\}$. Coordinatewise,
\[
 \min(0,u_i,v_i,u_i+v_i)=\min(0,u_i)+\min(0,v_i),
\]
so its height is $\rho(u)+\rho(v)\ge2r>h$, also impossible.
Thus each nontrivial fiber is a pair or a triple.
The padding description counts the edges of each direction.
A pair contributes one edge and one unit of defect, whereas
a triple contributes three edges and two units.
This gives \eqref{eq:edge_count}.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:rankone}
If the active rank is zero, then $|hA|=M_h$. If the active rank is
one, there is an integer $r$ with $2\le r\le h$ such that
\[
 |hA|=M_h-M_{h-r}.
\]
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Rank zero means that the representation map is injective.
For rank one, let $z$ be the primitive integer generator of the active
line. It belongs to $L_A$, and its degree $r$ is at most $h$.
Since the four elements are distinct, $r\ge2$.

Every fiber lies on a line parallel to $z$. Its integer points form
a consecutive chain: the parameters for which all four coordinates
are nonnegative form an interval. A fiber with $m$ representations
therefore has exactly $m-1$ consecutive edges, each with difference
$z$ up to sign. The displayed padding description counts all such
edges by $|U_{h-r}|=M_{h-r}$. Subtracting one per edge from the
$M_h$ representation points gives the result.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:short}
If $h\ge7$ and $0<\Delta_h(A)\le19$, then $r\ge h-2$,
every active relation is primitive, and there are at most four
unsigned active directions.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
For a primitive relation of degree $r$, the padded edges
$\gamma+z^-\leftrightarrow\gamma+z^+$ form disjoint chains in the
representation fibers. Even if a fiber contains more than one
chain, it loses at least as many values as there are chain edges.
Consequently
\[
 \Delta_h(A)\ge M_{h-r}.
\]
Since $M_3=20$, we have $r\ge h-2$.
A proper divisor of an active relation would have degree at most
$h/2<r$, so every active relation is primitive.

The active relations, together with zero, inject into $L/3L$.
Otherwise distinct vectors $u,v$ in this set would satisfy
\[
 0\ne (u-v)/3\in L,\qquad
 \rho((u-v)/3)\le 2h/3<h-2\le r.
\]
This contradicts the definition of $r$.
The group $L/3L$ has nine elements because $L$ has rank two.
There are therefore at most eight nonzero active vectors, or four
unsigned directions.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:fibers}
Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:short}, every representation
fiber has at most three points. There is at most one unsigned
active direction of degree $h-2$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
The fiber bound follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:fiber_tools},
since $2r\ge2(h-2)>h$.

Suppose two directions have degree $h-2$.
They contribute ten padded edges each. The graph formed by these
two directions is a forest in each fiber: a fiber has at most
three points, and a triangle uses three different directions.
The twenty edges therefore force defect at least twenty, a
contradiction.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:triangle}
Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:short}, at most one triangle
type and one orientation occur in degree $h$.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
By \eqref{eq:triangle_height_sum}, the heights of the two
orientations of one type satisfy
\[
 H+H'=\rho(u)+\rho(v)+\rho(u-v)\ge3(h-2)>2h.
\]
Thus both orientations cannot occur.

Two different triangle types, if present, share exactly two
directions: each uses three, and there are at most four in all.
Represent the shared directions by independent vectors $u,v$.
The other directions are $u+v$ and $u-v$, up to sign.
The four triangles obtained by deleting one corner of
$\{0,u,v,u+v\}$ represent the two orientations of these two types.
Put $R=\rho(u)+\rho(v)$. Deleting the indicated corner decreases
the parallelogram height by
\begin{align*}
 s_0&=\sum_i\min((u_i)_+,(v_i)_+),&
 s_u&=\sum_i\min((-u_i)_+,(v_i)_+),\\
 s_v&=\sum_i\min((u_i)_+,(-v_i)_+),&
 s_{u+v}&=\sum_i\min((-u_i)_+,(-v_i)_+).
\end{align*}
Here $x_+=\max(x,0)$.
These formulas follow by taking the coordinatewise minimum before
and after deleting the corner. The remaining triangle has height
$R-s_j$.

Opposite deleted corners give the same type. One triangle from
each type therefore corresponds to adjacent deleted corners.
Their two savings sum to at most $\rho(u)$ or $\rho(v)$, hence
at most $h$. For example,
$s_0+s_u\le\sum_i(v_i)_+=\rho(v)$; the other cases follow by
exchanging $u,v$ or changing their signs.
If both triangles fit in degree $h$, each saving is at least
$R-h$, giving $2R\le3h$.
But at most one of the shared directions has degree $h-2$, by
Lemma~\ref{lem:fibers}. Therefore
\[
 R\ge(h-2)+(h-1)=2h-3,\qquad 2R\ge4h-6>3h
\]
for $h\ge7$, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:small}
Let $h\ge7$ and $0\le\Delta_h(A)\le19$.
All active directions have degrees $h-2,h-1,h$, with respective
counts $\varepsilon,b,c$, where
\[
 \varepsilon\in\{0,1\},\qquad \varepsilon+b+c\le4.
\]
Every nontrivial representation fiber is a pair or a triple.
If $T$ is the number of triple fibers, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:small}
 \Delta_h(A)=10\varepsilon+4b+c-T,\qquad T\in\{0,1,4\}.
\end{equation}
If $T>0$, at least three directions occur; if $T=4$, at least
three of the directions have degree at most $h-1$.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Zero defect means that there are no active relations.
Otherwise the preceding lemmas apply. A triangle has height at
least $h-1$, since it uses three directions and at most one can
have smaller degree. Its height is thus $h-1$ or $h$ when it
occurs. The number of nonnegative common paddings is respectively
$M_1=4$ or $M_0=1$.

The padding rule following Lemma~\ref{lem:fiber_tools}, together
with Lemma~\ref{lem:triangle}, gives the possibilities for $T$.

The total number of collision edges is
$10\varepsilon+4b+c$. A pair fiber contributes one edge and one
unit of defect. A triple contributes three edges and two units.
Subtracting $T$ gives \eqref{eq:small}.
The last assertions follow from the three edges of a triangle
and from its height when $T=4$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:seventeen}
There are exactly three unsigned active relations, of degrees
$h-2,h-1,h-1$. There are fifteen pair fibers and one triple fiber.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
If $\varepsilon=0$ in \eqref{eq:small}, the defect is at most
$4(b+c)\le16$. Thus $\varepsilon=1$, and
\[
 17=10+4b+c-T,\qquad b+c\le3,\qquad T\in\{0,1,4\}.
\]
For $T=0,1,4$ this requires respectively $4b+c=7,8,11$.
The only solution with $b,c\ge0$ and $b+c\le3$ is
$(b,c,T)=(2,0,1)$. The eighteen edges therefore comprise three
edges of the triple and fifteen edges of pair fibers.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:basis}
The vectors $u,v$ form an integer basis of $L_A$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
They are independent; otherwise the fiber would contain an
equally spaced triple and an active multiple of an active vector.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:seventeen}, the full active set is
$\{\pm u,\pm v,\pm(v-u)\}$.
If the subgroup generated by $u,v$ had index greater than one,
its half-open fundamental parallelogram would contain a nonzero
point
\[
 w=\alpha u+\beta v\in L_A,\qquad 0\le\alpha,\beta<1.
\]
Replace $w$ by $u+v-w$ if $\alpha+\beta>1$.
Denote its coefficients again by $\alpha,\beta$; they now
satisfy $\alpha,\beta\ge0$ and $\alpha+\beta\le1$.
We obtain a nonvertex lattice point of the triangle
$\operatorname{conv}\{0,u,v\}$.
It cannot lie on a radial edge, since $u,v$ are primitive.
Its direction is therefore strictly inside their positive cone.
Convexity of $\rho$ gives
\[
 \rho(w)\le\alpha\rho(u)+\beta\rho(v)
 =\alpha(h-2)+\beta(h-1)
 \le(h-1)(\alpha+\beta)\le h-1.
\]
None of the six listed active vectors has this direction, a
contradiction.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:family}
For every integer $h\ge9$, the set $A_h$ in \eqref{eq:uniform}
is primitive and satisfies
\[
 \operatorname{diam}(A_h)=(h-3)(h-1),\qquad |hA_h|=M_h-17.
\]
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:Alist}
For the set $A(v,s)$, all nonzero relations of degree at
most $h=v+1$ are
\[
 \pm R,\quad \pm S,\quad \pm(R+S),
\]
where
\[
 R=(1,-u,u,-1),\qquad S=(1-v,v-s,s,-1).
\]
Their degrees are $h-2,h-1,h-1$, respectively.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The displayed vectors are relations, and their projections have
cross product $-(u-s,u+v-s,uv)$. They therefore form a full lattice
basis. Their degrees follow directly from the signs of their
coordinates; in particular,
$R+S=(2-v,2-s,u+s,-2)$ has degree $v$ because $s\le2$.

Write a short relation as $mR+nS$. Coordinates one and two sum
to $vn$. The absolute sum over any subset of coordinates is at
most the degree, so $v|n|\le v+1$. Thus $n\in\{-1,0,1\}$.
After changing sign, it suffices to consider $n=0,1$.

For $n=0$, the degree is $|m|(v-1)$, which forces $|m|\le1$.
For $n=1$, coordinate two is $um+s$. Its absolute value is at
most $v+1$. If $|m|\ge2$, then
\[
 |um+s|\ge u|m|-s\ge2u-s
 =2v-4-s\ge2v-6\ge v+2>v+1,
\]
where $u=v-2$, $v\ge8$ and $1\le s\le2$.
Thus $m\in\{-1,0,1\}$. The case $m=-1$ has degree
$\rho(S-R)=2v-2-s>v+1$ and is excluded. The remaining cases
give $S$ and $R+S$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:Blist}
For $B(v)$, all nonzero relations of degree at most $h=v+1$ are
\[
 \pm P,\quad \pm Q,\quad \pm(P+Q),
\]
where
\[
 P=(1-v,v,0,-1),\qquad Q=(2,1-v,u,-1).
\]
Their degrees are $h-1,h-1,h-2$, respectively.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Their projected cross product is $(u,2v-1,uv)$, so they are a
full lattice basis. The degrees follow from the coordinates,
including $P+Q=(3-v,1,u,-2)$.

For a short relation $mP+nQ$, coordinate two is $un$.
Since $2u>v+1$, we have $|n|\le1$. If $n=0$, then $|m|\le1$.
When $n=1$, coordinate one is $v(m-1)+1$, whose absolute bound
forces $m\in\{0,1,2\}$. At $m=2$, coordinate zero is $4-2v$,
with absolute value greater than $v+1$. Thus only $Q$ and
$P+Q$ remain. Sign symmetry treats $n=-1$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:large_ranktwo}
Let $A=\{0,a,b,D\}$ be normalized, with $D>d_h$ and active
rank two. Its least relation degree is at least $h-3$.
It has at most three unsigned active directions, and every
two independent active vectors form a basis of $L_A$.
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
Let $r$ be the least nonzero relation degree.
The active rank is two, so a shortest relation has an
independent active partner. If $r\le h-4$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:diameter} gives
\[
 D\le rh\le h(h-4)<d_h,
\]
a contradiction. Thus $r\ge h-3$.
The active vectors and zero inject into $L_A/3L_A$, as in
Lemma~\ref{lem:short}, since $2h/3<h-3$.
There are at most four unsigned directions. Every active
vector is primitive because $h/2<r$.

Suppose there are four directions.
A primitive lattice vector is nonzero modulo $2L_A$,
and its negative has the same residue.
The rank-two group $L_A/2L_A$ has only three nonzero classes,
so two representatives $p,q$ of different directions have
the same residue. They are independent.
Both $(p+q)/2$ and $(p-q)/2$ belong to $L_A$, so
the index of $\mathbb Z p+\mathbb Z q$ in $L_A$ is divisible by two.
The index factor in \eqref{eq:product_index} yields
\[
 2D\le\rho(p)\rho(q)\le h^2.
\]
But $d_h>h^2/2$ for $h\ge8$, contradicting $D>d_h$.
There are therefore at most three directions.

Finally, any independent active pair of index at least two
would give the same contradiction. Every such pair is a
full lattice basis.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:large_defects}
Under the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:large_ranktwo}, the
defect of $A$ is either a sum of at most three members of
$\{1,4,10,20\}$ or one of $17,23,26,29$.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
If there are three directions, let two be $u,v$, a lattice
basis by Lemma~\ref{lem:large_ranktwo}, and write the third
as $pu+qv$. Its pairs with $u$ and $v$ have indices
$|q|$ and $|p|$. Both are one. The third direction is
therefore $u+v$ or $u-v$, up to sign.
There is one triangle type.

Write the ordered degree deficits as $j_1\ge j_2$ in the
two-direction case, or $j_1\ge j_2\ge j_3$ in the three-direction
case: the degrees are $h-j_1,h-j_2,h-j_3$.
They lie in $\{h-3,h-2,h-1,h\}$.
The product of the two smallest degrees must exceed $d_h$,
which is equivalent to
\[
 (4-j_1-j_2)h+j_1j_2-3>0.
\]
For $h\ge17$ and $0\le j_2\le j_1\le3$, the possible pairs are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:degree_pairs}
 (j_1,j_2)\in
 \{(0,0),(1,0),(1,1),(2,0),(2,1),(2,2),(3,0)\}.
\end{equation}
The pair $(3,1)$ gives equality and is excluded.
If $j_1+j_2\ge5$, the product is smaller than $d_h$.

There are no active multiples and $2(h-3)>h$, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:fiber_tools} applies.
With two directions no triangle is possible, and the
defect is $M_{j_1}+M_{j_2}$.
With three directions, \eqref{eq:degree_pairs} leaves
\[
 0\le j_3\le j_2\le j_1\le2,\qquad\hbox{or}\qquad(j_1,j_2,j_3)=(3,0,0).
\]
The height sum of the two triangle orientations is at least
$3(h-3)>2h$. Hence at most one orientation occurs.
Its height is at least the largest edge degree $h-j_3$.
The padding count and \eqref{eq:edge_count} give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:large_defect_count}
 \Delta_h(A)=M_{j_1}+M_{j_2}+M_{j_3}-T,\qquad
 T\in\{0\}\cup\{M_0,\ldots,M_{j_3}\}.
\end{equation}
The nonzero corrections are listed in
Table~\ref{tab:exceptional}.
\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{Possible triple-fiber corrections for a large
representative. These are necessary cases, not an existence
claim for every degree configuration.}\label{tab:exceptional}
\begin{tabular}{ccc}
\toprule
$(j_1,j_2,j_3)$&Collision edges&Defects with $T>0$\\
\midrule
$(0,0,0)$&3&2\\
$(1,0,0)$&6&5\\
$(1,1,0)$&9&8\\
$(1,1,1)$&12&11,\ 8\\
$(2,0,0)$&12&11\\
$(2,1,0)$&15&14\\
$(2,1,1)$&18&17,\ 14\\
$(2,2,0)$&21&20\\
$(2,2,1)$&24&23,\ 20\\
$(2,2,2)$&30&29,\ 26,\ 20\\
$(3,0,0)$&22&21\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
Every entry except $17,23,26,29$ is a sum of at most two
members of $\{M_0,M_1,M_2,M_3\}=\{1,4,10,20\}$.
When $T=0$, the defect is already a sum of three such members.
This proves the proposition.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:principal_representative}
If the active rank is one and its primitive relation has
degree $r\le h-4$, its cardinality has a representative
of diameter less than $d_h$.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
By Lemma~\ref{lem:rankone}, the defect is $M_{h-r}$.
Use the principal representative
\cite[Section 10.2, (191)--(192)]{Shin}:
\[
 C_{h,r}=\{0,1,(r-1)h+1,(r-1)h+r\}.
\]
Put $m=(r-1)h+1$.
A short relation satisfies
\[
 m(z_2+z_3)+z_1+(r-1)z_3=0.
\]
The coefficients of the last expression lie in $[0,r-1]$,
so its absolute value is at most
$(r-1)\rho(z)\le(r-1)h<m$.
It follows that $z_2+z_3=0$ and every short relation is a
multiple of $(r-1,-(r-1),-1,1)$.
Thus $C_{h,r}$ has the required rank-one cardinality.
Its diameter is
\[
 (r-1)h+r\le h^2-4h-4<d_h.
\]
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:two_defects}
Let $h\ge17$ and $j_1,j_2\in\{-1,0,1,2,3\}$.
Put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:two_family}
 m=h-j_1-1,\qquad \ell=\lfloor m/2\rfloor,\qquad
 q=m(h-\ell)+\ell-j_2,\qquad A=\{0,1,q,q+m\}.
\end{equation}
Then $A$ is primitive,
\[
 \Delta_h(A)=M_{j_1}+M_{j_2},\qquad
 \operatorname{diam}(A)\le\tfrac12h^2+2h+\tfrac12<d_h.
\]
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
The set is increasing and primitive because $q>1$ and
it contains $0,1$.
For the relations, use the parametrization in
\cite[proof of Theorem 10.3, (189)--(190)]{Shin}.
For any homogeneous relation, set $s=z_2+z_3$ and $k=-z_3$.
The relation equation gives the unique parametrization
\begin{equation}\label{eq:two_relations}
 z=(e-s,-e,s+k,-k),\qquad e=qs-mk.
\end{equation}
For $s=0$, the primitive generator has degree $m+1=h-j_1$.
It is active exactly when $j_1\ge0$; its proper multiples
are inactive.

After changing sign, suppose $s\ge1$.
If $k<0$, then $e>q>h$, so the relation is not active.
For $k\ge0$, direct summation of the positive coordinates
in \eqref{eq:two_relations} gives
\[
 \rho(z)=s+k+\delta,\qquad
 \delta=\operatorname{dist}(e,[0,s]).
\]
Using $e=qs-mk$, we obtain
\[
 m\rho(z)-(q+m-1)s=m\delta-(e-s)\ge0.
\]
For $e\le s$, the last inequality follows from $\delta\ge0$.
For $e>s$, it is $(m-1)(e-s)\ge0$.
Thus every active relation with $s\ge1$ satisfies
\[
 (q+m-1)s\le mh.
\]
Write $p=m-2\ell\in\{0,1\}$.
Since $h-m=j_1+1$, substitution in \eqref{eq:two_family} yields
\[
 2(q+m-1)-mh=m(j_1+4+p)-p-2j_2-2>0.
\]
Indeed $m\ge h-4\ge13$, $j_1+4+p\ge3$, and
$p+2j_2+2\le9$.
It follows that $s=1$.

Let $L=h-\ell$.
At $k=L$, the value $e=\ell-j_2$ lies strictly between $1$
and $m$, and the degree is $h-j_2$.
At $k=L+1$, the degree is $h+p+j_2+2>h$.
At $k=L-1$, it is $h-j_2+m-1>h$.
As $k$ moves farther from $L$, the degree increases with
slope $m-1$ on the left and $m+1$ on the right.
There is therefore precisely one further active direction
when $j_2\ge0$, and none when $j_2=-1$.

There are at most two directions and no active multiples.
Since twice the smallest active degree exceeds $h$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:fiber_tools} applies, and no triple is possible.
Edge counting proves $\Delta_h(A)=M_{j_1}+M_{j_2}$, including
the case of no active relation.

Finally, $j_2\ge-1$ gives
\begin{align*}
 q+m
 &\le m(h+1)-(m-1)\ell+1\\
 &\le-\tfrac12m^2+(h+2)m+\tfrac12\\
 &\le\tfrac12h^2+2h+\tfrac12<d_h.
\end{align*}
The second inequality uses $\ell\ge(m-1)/2$.
For the third, the quadratic is increasing on $0\le m\le h$.
The last inequality holds for $h\ge17$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lem:three_defects}
Let $h\ge17$ and
$r_1,r_2,r_3\in\{h-3,h-2,h-1,h\}$.
Write $b=r_3$, and choose
\begin{equation}\label{eq:alpha_choice}
 \alpha=
 \begin{cases}
 (b-1)/2,&b\text{ odd},\\
 b/2-1,&b\equiv0\pmod4,\\
 b/2-2,&b\equiv2\pmod4.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
Put
\begin{equation}\label{eq:three_family}
 x=b-\alpha,\qquad \beta=r_1+\alpha-r_2,\qquad
 D=r_1b-\beta x,\qquad A=\{0,x,b,D\}.
\end{equation}
Then $A$ is primitive and
\[
 \Delta_h(A)=M_{h-r_1}+M_{h-r_2}+M_{h-r_3},\qquad
 D\le\tfrac34h^2+4<d_h.
\]
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
The choice \eqref{eq:alpha_choice} gives
\[
 b/2-2\le\alpha\le b/2,\qquad \gcd(\alpha,b)=1.
\]
For odd $b$, the gcd is immediate.
If $b\equiv0\pmod4$, it reduces to the gcd of an odd
number with two; if $b\equiv2\pmod4$, to the gcd of an
odd number with four.
Hence $0<x<b$ and $\gcd(x,b)=1$.

The identity
\begin{equation}\label{eq:D_convex}
 \frac Db=
 \frac{\alpha}{b}r_1+
 \left(1-\frac{\alpha}{b}\right)r_2-
 \alpha\left(1-\frac{\alpha}{b}\right)
\end{equation}
controls both the diameter and the possible relations.
The first two terms form a convex combination of numbers
in $[h-3,h]$. Moreover,
\[
 \frac b4-\frac4b
 \le\alpha(1-\alpha/b)\le\frac b4.
\]
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:three_bounds}
 D/b\ge3h/4-3>h/2,\qquad
 D\le hb-b^2/4+4\le3h^2/4+4<d_h.
\end{equation}
The upper bound uses that $hb-b^2/4$ is increasing for
$0\le b\le h$. In particular, $D>b$ and $A$ is a
primitive four-set.

To list the active relations, first note that
\begin{align}
 |Dz_3|
 &=|xz_1+bz_2|
   =|x(z_1+z_2)+\alpha z_2|\notag\\
 &\le x|z_1+z_2|+\alpha|z_2|
 \le(x+\alpha)h=bh. \label{eq:lastcoord}
\end{align}
The last inequality is the subset-mass bound
\eqref{eq:subsetmass}. Together with $D>bh/2$, it gives
$|z_3|\le1$.

For $z_3=0$, the primitive generator is
\[
 R=(-\alpha,b,-x,0),\qquad \rho(R)=b.
\]
Its proper multiples are inactive.
For $z_3=1$, every relation is $S+kR$, where
\begin{equation}\label{eq:three_S}
 S=(r_2-\alpha-1,\beta,-r_1,1).
\end{equation}
This follows from $\gcd(x,b)=1$ and the relation equation.
The bounds on $\alpha$ and the $r_i$ give
$r_2-\alpha-1>0$, $\beta>0$, $\beta<b$ and $x<r_1$.
Thus
\[
 \rho(S)=r_1,\qquad
 S-R=(r_2-1,\beta-b,x-r_1,1),\qquad
 \rho(S-R)=r_2.
\]

For $k\ge1$, coordinate two of $S+kR$ is $-r_1-kx$.
Its absolute value is at least
\[
 r_1+x\ge(h-3)+(h-3)/2=\tfrac32h-\tfrac92>h.
\]
For $k\le-2$, coordinate one has absolute value at least
\[
 2b-\beta\ge\tfrac32(h-3)-3=\tfrac32h-\tfrac{15}2>h.
\]
Hence the complete active list is
$\pm R,\pm S,\pm(S-R)$.

The two triangle heights are
\[
 H=r_1+\alpha,\qquad H'=r_2+b-\alpha.
\]
Both exceed $h$: they are at least
$3h/2-13/2$ and $3h/2-6$, respectively.
There are no triple fibers.
Lemma~\ref{lem:fiber_tools} and the three relation degrees
now give the asserted defect.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lem:special_three}
For every $h\ge17$, the defects $23,26,29$ have
integer four-set representatives of diameter at most $d_h$.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Most cases use \eqref{eq:three_family} with a smaller value
of $\alpha$. The parameters are listed in
Table~\ref{tab:special_params}.
\begin{table}[H]
\centering
\caption{Specializations of $\{0,b-\alpha,b,r_1b-\beta(b-\alpha)\}$,
where $\beta=r_1+\alpha-r_2$.}\label{tab:special_params}
\setlength{\tabcolsep}{4pt}
\begin{tabular}{ccccccc}
\toprule
Defect&Condition&$r_1$&$r_2$&$b$&$\alpha$&$D$\\
\midrule
23&$h$ even&$h-2$&$h-2$&$h-1$&2&$h^2-5h+8$\\
23&$h$ odd&$h-2$&$h-1$&$h-2$&2&$h^2-5h+8$\\
26&all $h$&$h-2$&$h-2$&$h-2$&1&$h^2-5h+7$\\
29&$h$ odd&$h-2$&$h-2$&$h-2$&2&$h^2-6h+12$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
Each set is primitive: either $\alpha=1$, or $\alpha=2$
and $b$ is odd. All displayed diameters are less than $d_h$.

The parametrization \eqref{eq:three_S} remains valid.
Here $D/b\ge h-4>h/2$, so \eqref{eq:lastcoord} again gives
$|z_3|\le1$.
For $k\ge1$, coordinate two of $S+kR$ has absolute value
at least $r_1+x\ge2h-6>h$.
For $k\le-2$, coordinate one has absolute value at least
$2b-\beta\ge2h-6>h$.
The complete active list is therefore
$\pm R,\pm S,\pm(S-R)$, with degrees $b,r_1,r_2$.
Their triangle heights are $H=r_1+\alpha$ and
$H'=r_2+b-\alpha$.
In the four rows of the table, $H$ is respectively
$h,h,h-1,h$, while $H'>h$.
There are respectively $1,1,4,1$ triple fibers.
The edge totals are $24,24,30,30$, so the defects are
$23,23,26,29$ as required.

It remains to realize defect twenty-nine when $h$ is even.
Put $n=h-4$ and $k=n/2$, and choose
\begin{equation}\label{eq:even_t}
 t=
 \begin{cases}
 k+1,&k\text{ even},\\
 k-2,&k\text{ odd}.
 \end{cases}
\end{equation}
Since even $h\ge17$ means $h\ge18$, we have $n\ge14$
and $1\le t\le n$.
Let
\begin{equation}\label{eq:even_29}
 D=n^2+2n+2,\qquad
 a=D-(n+1)t-n,\qquad b=D-nt+2,\qquad A=\{0,a,b,D\}.
\end{equation}
Then $a\ge2$, $b-a=t+n+2>0$, $b<D$, and
$D<d_h=n^2+4n+3$.

We check primitivity before using the relation vectors.
The gcd of the set entries is
\[
 \gcd(D,nt-2,(n+1)t+n)=\gcd(D,t+n+2).
\]
Indeed, subtracting the last two entries gives $t+n+2$.
Conversely, if a divisor of $D$ divides $t+n+2$, then
$t\equiv-n-2$ modulo that divisor, and
$nt-2\equiv-n^2-2n-2=-D$.
This proves the reverse divisibility.

For even $k$, $t+n+2=3(k+1)$; for odd $k$, it is $3k$.
Now $D=(2k+1)^2+1$ is not divisible by three.
In the first case,
$\gcd(D,k+1)=\gcd(2,k+1)=1$ because $k+1$ is odd.
In the second, $\gcd(D,k)=\gcd(2,k)=1$ because $k$ is odd.
Thus $A$ is primitive in every even order.

Consider
\[
 P=(1+t,1,n+2-t,0),\quad
 Q=(1,n+1,0,2),\quad R=(0,0,2,n+2).
\]
These exponent vectors refer to the coordinate order
$(0,b,D,a)$. Their degree is $h=n+4$.
The differences
\[
 u=Q-P=(-t,n,t-n-2,2),\qquad
 v=R-P=(-1-t,-1,t-n,n+2)
\]
have projected cross product $(-b,-D,-a)$.
By the primitivity just proved, they form a full basis
of the relation lattice.

For a relation $z=iu+jv$, coordinates one and three are
\[
 z_1=ni-j,\qquad z_3=2i+(n+2)j.
\]
The coefficient matrix has determinant $D$, so an active
relation satisfies
\[
 |i|\le\frac{(n+3)(n+4)}D<2,\qquad
 |j|\le\frac{(n+2)(n+4)}D<2.
\]
Both inequalities hold for $n\ge14$.
Thus $i,j\in\{-1,0,1\}$.
The vectors $u,v,u-v$ have degree $n+2=h-2$,
whereas $u+v$ has degree $2n+3>h$.
These three unsigned directions are the complete active list.

The common coordinate minimum of $P,Q,R$ is zero, so
their triangle has height $h$.
The opposite orientation has height $3(h-2)-h=2h-6>h$.
There is exactly one triple fiber.
The defect is therefore $3M_2-1=29$.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:uniform_upper}
For every integer $h\ge17$, $\nu(h,4)\le(h-3)(h-1)$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Use Lemma~\ref{lem:replacement} with $D_0=d_h$.
Take a normalized representative $A$ with diameter greater
than $d_h$.
If its active rank is zero, or is one with relation degree
at least $h-3$, its defect is $0,1,4,10$ or $20$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:two_defects} provides a short representative
of the same cardinality.
If the active rank is one with smaller degree,
Lemma~\ref{lem:principal_representative} does so.

For active rank two,
Proposition~\ref{prop:large_defects} leaves sums of at most
three members of $\{1,4,10,20\}$ and the four defects
$17,23,26,29$.
Lemmas~\ref{lem:two_defects} and \ref{lem:three_defects}
handle the basic sums.
Proposition~\ref{thm:family} handles seventeen, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:special_three} handles the other special defects.
Every replacement has the same sumset cardinality and
diameter at most $d_h$, as required.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:finite}
The values of $\nu(h,4)$ for $2\le h\le20$ are given in
Table~\ref{tab:finite}. In this range,
\[
 \nu(h,4)=D_h^{\max}\quad(2\le h\le10),\qquad
 \nu(h,4)=(h-3)(h-1)\quad(11\le h\le20).
\]
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:coverage}
Let $C\ge h^2$, and enumerate all four-sets in $[0,C]\cap\mathbb Z$.
If their cardinalities include
\begin{equation}\label{eq:taillist}
 \{M_h\}\ \cup\
 \{M_h-M_{h-r}:2\le r\le h\},
\end{equation}
then the enumeration contains every element of $\mathcal R(h,4)$.
The largest of the enumerated minimum realizing diameters is
$\nu(h,4)$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Normalize an arbitrary realizing set. If its diameter is greater
than $C$, Lemma~\ref{lem:diameter} forces active rank at most one,
and Lemma~\ref{lem:rankone} places its cardinality in
\eqref{eq:taillist}. Those cardinalities are already present.
For each cardinality, the enumeration includes a representative of
its true minimum diameter: any smaller one would also be inside the
enumerated interval.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
